title: GraphQL Fundamentals
summary: One endpoint, client-specified response shape — and the N+1 query problem that shows up the moment resolvers naively fan out to fetch nested data.

slides.markdown:
**GraphQL** flips the usual API model: instead of many fixed endpoints each returning a fixed shape, there's **one endpoint**, and the client sends a query describing exactly which fields it wants — across however many underlying resources those fields come from.

Think of it like ordering à la carte instead of picking from a set menu: you name the exact dishes (fields) you want from across the kitchen (services), and one order (request) brings them all back together. The power comes at a cost — a naive server implementation can turn one client query into hundreds of backend calls, which this topic gets to.

slides.sectionTitle: One endpoint, client-specified shape: the GraphQL model
slides.markdown:
A GraphQL API exposes a single endpoint, usually `POST /graphql`. Every request carries a **query** — not a URL path — that names exactly which fields the client wants: `{ user(id: 42) { name, orders { id, total } } }` asks for a user's name plus their orders' id and total, nothing else.

This is the opposite of REST, where the server decides each endpoint's response shape ahead of time and the client takes what it gets (or calls several endpoints and stitches results together itself). In GraphQL, the client decides the shape at request time, and the server assembles exactly that response.

The result: a mobile app's list view and a web app's detail view can hit the same endpoint and each get precisely the fields they need, instead of maintaining separate REST endpoints per view.

A GraphQL API is defined by a **schema**: a strongly-typed description of every object (`type User { id: ID!, name: String!, orders: [Order!]! }`), its fields, and the operations (queries, mutations) a client can perform. The schema is the contract clients code against — much like a `.proto` file for gRPC, but queryable and introspectable at runtime.

Behind each field sits a **resolver** — a small function that knows how to fetch that specific field's value, often from a different backend than its parent field. `User.orders`'s resolver might call an entirely separate Orders service, while `User.name` reads straight from a cache.

This separation is what makes the "one query, many sources" model work: the schema tells the client what's queryable, and resolvers are the server-side plumbing that stitches together wherever the data actually lives.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a single GraphQL query resolving fields from multiple services
slides.markdown:
![One GraphQL query fanning out to three services and merging into one response](assets/graphql-resolver-fanout.svg)

One client request hits the GraphQL server, which parses the query, and for each requested field calls the resolver responsible for it — some fields resolve locally, others call out to entirely separate services. All the results merge into a single response the client receives as one JSON object, with no awareness of how many backend calls happened underneath.

This fan-out is exactly where the N+1 problem (a few slides ahead) originates: each resolver call is cheap in isolation, but the count of them can explode.

assets.alt: One GraphQL query fanning out to three services and merging into one response

slides.markdown:
**Over-fetching** is a REST client receiving fields it doesn't need — a mobile list row asking `GET /users/42` and getting back a full profile with fields it'll never render. **Under-fetching** is the opposite: the first response doesn't have everything the screen needs, so the client fires off follow-up requests (`GET /users/42/orders`, `GET /users/42/preferences`) to assemble the full picture.

GraphQL solves both with the same mechanism: the client's query names exactly the fields it wants, from exactly the related objects it needs, in one round trip. No unused fields come back, and no follow-up requests are needed to fill gaps — the nested `orders { id, total }` inside a `user` query is what would have been a second REST call.

This is the single biggest reason product teams reach for GraphQL: fewer round trips, and a response shaped to the screen instead of the server's convenience.

slides.sectionTitle: The N+1 query problem and batching/dataloader fixes
slides.markdown:
The **N+1 problem**: a query asks for 50 users and each user's `orders` field. A naive resolver fetches the 50 users in one query (1), then calls the `orders` resolver once *per user* (N=50), issuing 50 separate database or service calls — 51 total round trips for what should be a couple.

The standard fix is a **DataLoader** (or equivalent batching layer): instead of each `orders` resolver call hitting the database immediately, it queues its request and the loader batches everything queued within the same tick into one call — `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (1,2,3,...,50)` — then hands each resolver its own slice of the result.

The resolver code doesn't change conceptually; the batching happens transparently underneath, turning 51 round trips back into roughly 2.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: GraphQL vs REST — flexibility vs caching/simplicity
slides.markdown:
| | GraphQL | REST |
|---|---|---|
| Response shape | Client-specified, exact fields | Server-fixed per endpoint |
| Round trips for nested data | One | Often several (under-fetching) |
| HTTP caching (CDN, browser) | Hard — usually one POST endpoint | Easy — GET + URL is cacheable by default |
| Learning curve / tooling | Schema, resolvers, N+1 awareness required | Simple mental model, mature tooling everywhere |
| Risk surface | A deeply nested query can be expensive server-side | Each endpoint's cost is roughly fixed and known |

**How to decide:** GraphQL earns its complexity when clients have genuinely varied data needs (many device types, rapidly changing UIs) and round-trip count matters. REST stays simpler and easier to cache when the API's consumers have fairly uniform, predictable needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a naive resolver chain causing an N+1 explosion
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Each resolver only does one small, cheap thing, so the API is fast."

**Why it's wrong:** cheap-per-call doesn't mean cheap-in-total. A query for 100 users' `orders` field, with no batching, issues 100 separate calls to the orders backend — each one fast in isolation, but 100 round trips is still 100 round trips, and it gets worse the deeper the query nests (users → orders → line items → products could multiply into thousands of calls).

**Correct model:** every resolver that fetches related data by a parent's ID is a batching candidate. Wire a DataLoader (or equivalent) into any resolver where the client's query could plausibly request the field for many parents at once — which, in a schema with nested relationships, is most of them.

slides.sectionTitle: Query complexity and depth limiting: guarding against expensive queries
slides.subTitle: Production hardening
slides.markdown:
Because a GraphQL client can request arbitrarily deep and wide queries against your schema, a single query can accidentally (or maliciously) demand far more work than a REST endpoint ever could — nested queries can fan out into thousands of resolver calls even after dataloader batching fixes N+1.

Production servers guard against this with **query complexity analysis** (assign each field a cost, sum the total, reject queries above a budget — e.g., 1,000 points per request) and **depth limiting** (reject queries nested more than, say, 6-8 levels deep). Some APIs also enforce per-field rate limits separately from the endpoint-level rate limit, since one expensive field (e.g., a full-text search resolver) can dominate cost even in a shallow query.

The takeaway: REST's per-endpoint rate limiting doesn't transfer directly to GraphQL — a single endpoint (`/graphql`) can hide wildly different costs per request, so cost has to be measured per-query, not per-route.
